$note: Real, measured results from a one-off 100M-row benchmark run on the dev sandbox this was built on (16.95 GB total RAM, ~2.25 GB available at benchmark time, ~21 GB free disk). Not re-generated automatically -- re-run via `python -m app.large_data.benchmark_100m <command>` (see module docstring) or `RUN_100M_BENCHMARK=1 pytest tests/test_large_data_100m.py` to refresh on different hardware.

chunked_read.finding: Memory stays bounded (125.65 MB) regardless of the 100M-row scale -- confirms chunked_reader.py's core claim holds at this scale, not just at the previously-tested 10M.

chunked_aggregate.finding: Full groupby-sum over 100M rows, memory still bounded at ~126 MB.

BEFORE_FIX.finding: reservoir_sample_csv was ~87x slower than chunked_read over the same file -- a real performance bug, not expected/acceptable overhead. Root cause: a per-winner `.iloc[slot] = ...` pandas scalar assignment inside a Python loop -- the winner *count* was small as designed, but pandas' per-call constant-factor overhead for scalar .iloc assignment dominates at this row count.

AFTER_FIX.fix: Batched all of a chunk's reservoir winners into a single vectorized `.iloc[fancy_index] = values` assignment instead of a per-winner loop. Verified numpy/pandas fancy-index assignment applies 'last write wins' for duplicate target indices, exactly matching the original per-row sequential-loop semantics -- a pure performance fix, zero behavior change. All pre-existing correctness/determinism tests (test_large_data.py) pass unmodified.

sql_bridge_current_system.reason: app.sql.duckdb_source.DuckDBDataSource takes an in-memory pandas DataFrame today, not a file path -- querying via the existing bridge requires full materialization first. A full 100M-row pandas DataFrame needs ~9.2 GB (see naive_load_ceiling below), far beyond this machine's ~2.25 GB available RAM at benchmark time -- not attempted, to avoid an OS-level crash/thrash. This is a real, current architectural boundary of the SQL bridge, not a bug -- documented, not silently assumed to scale.

naive_load_ceiling_extrapolated.note: LINEAR EXTRAPOLATION from a real 2M-row measurement (in a fresh process, separate from generation, to avoid peak-RSS contamination), NOT a measurement at 100M rows. Confirms a full in-memory load at 100M rows would need ~9.2 GB, well beyond the ~2.25 GB available on this machine at benchmark time.

duckdb_direct_csv_FORWARD_LOOKING.note: DuckDB querying the 100M-row CSV FILE DIRECTLY via read_csv_auto, completely bypassing pandas -- NOT what the shipped DuckDBDataSource does today (see sql_bridge_current_system above). Dramatically faster than the pandas-chunked approach for the same data (5.56s/6.69s vs 70.71s/149.56s) using only a 1 GB DuckDB memory limit. Strong forward-looking evidence for a future architectural decision: migrating the SQL bridge to stream directly from disk via DuckDB instead of requiring an in-memory DataFrame first.

memory_guard_failure_recovery.finding: A deliberately undersized chunk-byte ceiling correctly raises a clean, actionable error rather than crashing or silently truncating -- confirmed graceful failure recovery.

truncated_file_failure_recovery.finding: A CSV truncated mid-final-row does NOT raise and does NOT drop the partial row -- pandas keeps it as an extra row with the missing trailing fields read as NaN. Silent, not a crash -- worth knowing (a truncated source file produces a partially-NaN row, not an error) but not itself a bug given this project's tools already treat NaN as missing data throughout.
